rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.1-2.2 and Abstract: three-year field experiment (2012-2014) at Shihezi, Xinjiang, with five fertilizer levels x three drip irrigation levels in a randomised factorial design; own measurements of LAI, dry matter, seed cotton yield, WUE, PFP and economic benefits (Tables 2-4, Figs 2-3).
rows.notes: All treatments are drip-fertigated under plastic mulch; the study compares irrigation amounts (0.6, 0.8, 1.0 ETc) and fertilizer rates within drip, with no non-drip comparison. It therefore shows how yield, WUE and PFP respond to water and fertilizer amounts under drip (yield and PFP highest at 1.0 ETc; yield maximised at 300-120-60 kg/ha N-P2O5-K2O; optimum intervals 362-462 mm and 212.5-85-42.5 to 367.5-147-73.5 kg/ha via regression), not that drip itself improves yield, quality or water/fertilizer productivity relative to another technology. Fibre quality was not measured. Standard errors (n=3) are given for yield/LAI figures but do not apply because Q2 is no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2.1-2.2 and Abstract: three-year field experiment (2012-2014) at Shihezi, Xinjiang, with five fertilizer levels x three drip irrigation levels; own measurements of WUE (Table 3), irrigation amounts (Table 1) and economic benefits (Table 4).
rows.notes: The study does not test drip against any other irrigation method, so it provides no result of its own on drip being water-saving or high-efficiency. What it shows is that, within drip fertigation, WUE was lowest at full irrigation (1.0 ETc) and higher under deficit levels (0.6-0.8 ETc), while reduced irrigation cut yield and economic benefits substantially (Section 3.3-3.4, 4.2); the authors note farmers have weak willingness to save water because the water fee is a small share of costs. This is evidence about irrigation amount under drip, not about drip as a water-conservation technology.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a water x fertilizer factorial trial entirely under mulched drip fertigation at a single site with one soil (sandy loam) and two early-maturing cultivars; drip irrigation is the common platform, not a treatment factor, so it cannot be evidence that drip delivers yield, quality or water-saving benefits relative to other technologies.
